reason: Jung's own apposition 'the albedo, the moonlight' equates albedo with moonlight (Luna's light), and rubedo/Sol is set against it later in the paragraph. Quote accurate; only the 'heralds the rising sun' part is attributed to 'some alchemists', the albedo=moonlight gloss is Jung's. Direction fine.

Paragraph twice ties rubedo to consciousness in Jung's own voice: 'light coming from the sun, consciousness' and 'This corresponds to the increasing participation of consciousness.' Quote accurate, direction correct, jung-asserts is right.

Jung states flatly in his own voice: 'For Mercurius is the light-bringing Nous, who knows the secret of transformation and of immortality.' This is Jung's assertion (explaining why the Maier encounter is significant), not a quoted alchemist, so jung-asserts holds. Quote exact.

Opening sentence is Jung's own comparison: aqua pontica/permanens 'behaves very much like the baptismal water of the Church', elaborated through the whole paragraph (ablution, baptism in fire, solutio as burial/rebirth). 'Parallels' correctly renders 'behaves very much like' without overclaiming identity.

Jung's own gloss on the opus stage: 'the solutio, which signifies the total dissolution of the imperfect body in the aqua divina, its submersion, mortification, and burial.' Direction correct (solutio dissolves the body). Quote accurate.

Quote accurate and direction correct, but claim_type is wrong. Jung's 'so salt is a synonym for the arcane substance' is his inference from the 'Gloria mundi' passage he has just quoted ('salt takes its origin from Mercurius'); it is a report of alchemical terminology, not a psychological assertion in Jung's own name. Per project rule, reported alchemical designations of salt must not be jung-asserts.
'Salt as much as ash is a synonym for the albedo (or dealbatio)' — quote accurate, footnoted to an alchemical source, and correctly tagged jung-reports-parallel. Direction fine.

Two problems. (1) The quote strips the frame 'when we are informed, further, that...' — the meaning 'soul' is reported from the alchemical texts (the 'Gloria mundi': 'The salt of the earth is the soul'), so jung-asserts is wrong. (2) Object overreach: the text says 'soul' (anima/soul, human soul, anima mundi), not 'the psyche' as a whole; the paragraph pointedly treats this soul as transcendental and ambiguous, so widening it to 'psyche' is a conflation.

Text: 'the "salt of our magnesia" is a "spark of the anima mundi"' — both phrases in quotation marks with source footnotes, correctly tagged jung-reports-parallel. Slight compression of 'salt of our magnesia' to salt is acceptable inside a paragraph enumerating the significations of salt. Direction correct.
'For Glauber the salt is feminine and corresponds to Eve.' Quote accurate, correctly attributed to Glauber as jung-reports-parallel, direction correct.

'Glauber himself makes the equation Sal:Sol = A:Omega, so that salt becomes an analogue of God.' Quote accurate; correctly tagged jung-reports-parallel with source Glauber. Text says 'God', not 'God-image', but mapping to the god-image node is the correct graph normalization for a reported God-analogy and does not misstate the claim.

'Without salt the work has no success' is given as Khunrath's statement (fn 656), and the whole paragraph piles up sources on salt's necessity for the opus ('No man can understand this Art who does not know the salt'). jung-quotes-source with source Khunrath is exactly right. Direction correct.

'"It is certain," says Dorn, "that a salt, the natural balsam of the body, is begotten from human blood."' Quote accurate, correctly attributed to Dorn as jung-quotes-source, direction correct (salt begotten FROM blood).
'Mylius expressly identifies salt with the uroboros-dragon' — Jung reporting Mylius's identification (fn 672). Quote accurate, claim_type jung-reports-parallel with source Mylius is correct.

'he has become the carrier of a myth, that is to say, of the statements of the collective unconscious' — Jung's own assertion; direction correct (rex carries CU content, not vice versa). Note the object is strictly 'a myth, i.e. the statements of the collective unconscious', a faithful compression.

Quote accurate but claim_type and scope are wrong. 'It is clear from this and from the text that follows that... the king is none other than gold' is Jung's exegesis of the Zosimos passage (the earliest king reference in alchemy), not a standing identity Jung asserts of Rex generally. The same paragraph immediately qualifies: the gold in question is the 'philosophic' gold, 'aurum non vulgi', an embodiment of psyche and pneuma. Flat 'rex is gold' as jung-asserts is identity overreach.

Direction and claim_type fine, but the subject is too broad. The text says the 'philosophic' gold — 'an aurum non vulgi, a living gold, so to speak, which corresponds in every respect to the lapis' — explicitly distinguished from common gold. Attaching the edge to the generic Gold (aurum) node conflates aurum vulgi with aurum philosophicum.

'the king, like every archetype, is not just a static image; he signifies a dynamic process' — Jung directly classes the king among archetypes, in his own voice. Quote accurate. Minor caveat: the node label's parenthetical 'archetype-as-such' is technically the wrong register (the king is an archetypal image, not the archetype an sich), but the edge rex is-a archetype matches the text.

'The transformation of the king... is portrayed in a similar manner in alchemy. It describes either his procreation and birth, in the form of a hierosgamos, or else his... rebirth in perfect form.' Hierosgamos is one of the two portrayed modes of the king's transformation; the edge is a fair rendering. Quote accurate, jung-asserts correct.

'This parable contains the primitive motif of the murder or sacrifice of the king for the purpose of renewing his kingly power' — direction correct (the king undergoes the sacrifice), reinforced later: 'the old king had either to die or to offer sacrifice.' Quote accurate, jung-asserts fine.

'The dissolution of the heart in water would therefore correspond to the union of the male with the female, and this in turn to the union of conscious and unconscious' — Jung's own psychological equation of the (Dornian, spiritual) solutio with the union of opposites/spagyric marriage. Quote accurate, direction fine, jung-asserts appropriate.

Direction correct and the quote is verbatim, but the object drops the decisive qualifier: 'the king personifies a hypertrophy of the ego which calls for compensation' (in the Allegoria Merlini). Rex here personifies the inflated/hypertrophied ego needing dissolution, not the ego as such — the compensation logic depends on that qualifier.
